title: How The FBI Hunted A Mob Boss For 16 Years With A TV Ad Aimed At His Girlfriend
sources: FBI.gov: Top Ten Fugitive James 'Whitey' Bulger Arrested (23 Jun 2011); FBI Los Angeles: Most Wanted Fugitive Bulger Captured in Santa Monica
History.com This Day in History 22 Jun (Greig PSA aired 20 Jun 2011); NPR 23 Jun 2011
US v. Bulger trial record 2013 (31 counts, 11 murders found); Wikipedia: Whitey Bulger; Catherine Greig; John Connolly (FBI); Stephen Flemmi

Hedged in script: LSD tests (Bulger's own claim), Connolly as tip source (court testimony), storage-locker lure (agents' account), Iceland tipster + reward (later reports), London box (investigators' belief); Connolly's later Florida case not detailed

beats.text: Santa Monica, California. A quiet apartment building three blocks from the ocean.
An old man with a white beard and a white hat walks down to the garage. He has been told his storage locker was broken into.
He is eighty-one years old. Neighbours know him as Charlie Gasko, a polite retired man who walks on the beach with his wife.
But the people waiting for him in that garage are federal agents.
And the old man is James Bulger. Whitey. For sixteen years, one of the most wanted men in America.
What found him was not a wiretap or a fingerprint. It was a daytime TV ad. And it was not about him at all.
To see why, we go back to Boston, to the neighbourhood that made him.
Bulger was born in 1929 and grew up in a housing project in South Boston.
As a young man he robbed banks, and in 1956 he was sent to federal prison.
He served time in Atlanta, at Leavenworth, and at Alcatraz. By his own account, in Atlanta he volunteered for secret government LSD tests.
He came home in 1965. His younger brother William was starting a career in politics. He would one day lead the Massachusetts State Senate.
Whitey went the other way. By the late 1970s he and his partner Stephen Flemmi ran the Winter Hill Gang.
Prosecutors would later say they ran loan sharking, gambling, drug dealing and extortion, and that they killed people who got in the way.
So why did nobody stop them? Because Whitey Bulger had a secret.
Since 1975 he had been an informant for the FBI.
His handler was an agent named John Connolly, who grew up in the same projects.
The official idea was to use Bulger against the Italian Mafia in Boston. And the Mafia did take heavy blows.
But in court, years later, it came out that the protection ran both ways. Agents leaked secrets to Bulger and looked away from his crimes.
Connolly retired in 1990. He was later convicted and sent to prison for what he did.
By 1994, a team of state police, the DEA and federal prosecutors was building a racketeering case that the Boston FBI office did not control.
In December, Bulger got the warning. Indictments were coming. Court testimony later named Connolly as the source.
On December twenty-third, 1994, he left Boston with his girlfriend Theresa Stanley. This is day one.
Within weeks Stanley wanted to go home. So he drove back, dropped her off, and picked up a different woman.
Her name was Catherine Greig. A dental hygienist, about twenty years younger, who had loved him for years.
On January fifth, 1995, police arrested Flemmi in Boston. Whitey was already gone. Day fourteen.
Later Flemmi learned his partner had been an informant all along. And in time, he started telling the government everything.
Bulger had planned for this for years. He carried fake identities and kept cash hidden in different places.
In August 1999 he was added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list. Day 1,701.

v.q: FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives poster

beats.text: The reward climbed to one million dollars, and later two million. For years only Osama bin Laden ranked above him on that list.
Tips poured in from all over the world. People saw him in Europe, in Mexico, in small towns all over America.
In 2002 investigators believed he had been in London, and they traced a safe deposit box there.
But the trail went cold, year after year.
The FBI's own history with him made it worse. Critics asked if the Bureau really wanted to find the man who could embarrass it.
Then a new fugitive task force took over the hunt and tried something different.
Bulger had spent sixteen years hiding his own face. So stop chasing his face. Chase hers.
Greig had habits a man on the run could not control. She was careful about her teeth and her looks, and she loved animals.
The people who might meet her were dentists, hair salons, vets, and the women who watch daytime TV.
So the FBI made a short public service ad about Catherine Greig, and on June twentieth, 2011, it started running in cities across the country. Day 6,024.
It ran during daytime shows. The message was simple: this woman is with a fugitive. Have you seen her?
The next evening, just after eight o'clock, a tip reached the FBI's Los Angeles office. Day 6,025.
By later reports, the tip came from a woman who had seen the story far away, in Iceland.
She had once lived in Santa Monica and knew the couple from the neighbourhood, and the stray cat they fed.
She was later reported to have received the two million dollar reward.
Agents moved fast. The address was an apartment block on Third Street called the Princess Eugenia.
The couple had lived there since around 1996, almost the whole time Boston was looking for them.
Agents did not want to storm an apartment where a gangster might be armed. So they asked the manager to help.
According to the agents' account, he was told his storage locker had been broken into. He came down to the garage.
June twenty-second, 2011. Day 6,026. The agents surrounded him, and Whitey Bulger was arrested without a shot.
Greig was arrested inside the apartment.
Then came the search. Hidden in the walls, agents found more than eight hundred thousand dollars in cash.
And about thirty guns. Fake IDs. Disguises. Sixteen years of planning, in one small apartment.
So how did a man that careful live so openly? He was not hiding in a forest. He was in plain sight, in a nice beach town.
He walked every day, he was polite, and he never stood out. The disguise was being boring.
But Greig was the part he could not disguise. A face people remembered from the street, from the neighbourhood, from feeding a stray cat.
He was flown back to Boston, and in 2013 his trial began in the federal courthouse on the harbour.
Flemmi and other former partners testified against him.
Bulger said he had never been an informant. The FBI's own file said otherwise.
In August 2013 the jury found him guilty on thirty-one counts, and found that he took part in eleven murders.

v.q: John Joseph Moakley Federal Courthouse Boston

beats.text: He was sentenced to two life terms plus five years.
Catherine Greig pleaded guilty to helping him hide and was sentenced to eight years in prison.
In 2018, at eighty-nine, Bulger was killed in a federal prison in West Virginia, soon after he was moved there.
His story led to hearings, lawsuits, and a long hard look at how the FBI handles informants.
So what really caught Whitey Bulger?
Not the reward. Not the sightings. Not his own face.
A short ad aimed at the woman next to him, and a neighbour thousands of miles away who happened to be watching.
Sixteen years. Six thousand and twenty-six days. And barely two days once they changed the question.
